theory_name: Generalized dynamical theory of thermoelasticity with one relaxation time (Lord-Shulman theory)
heat_law_equation_ref: eq (8), printed p.300; general anisotropic form eq (7), printed p.300; Fourier limit eq (6), printed p.300
heat_law_in_words: Isotropic form (8): q_i + tau0 dq_i/dt = -k T_,i, the heat flux and its time derivative being linearly related to the temperature gradient; (7) is the general tensor form with a_ij on the rate term and B_ij on the gradient. Eq (6), q_i = -k T_,i, is recovered as the limit in which the rate term is dropped.
relaxation_parameters: tau0, called the relaxation time, eq (8), printed p.300, defined as 'the time-lag needed to establish steady-state heat conduction in an element of volume when a temperature gradient is suddenly imposed'; its non-dimensional form beta, called the relaxation constant, eq (30), printed p.303
wave_speed_or_dispersion_ref: printed pp.306-307 (PDF pp.8-9): the solutions (44) and (46) contain two wave fronts; the thermal front travels at the constant non-dimensional velocity 1/sqrt(beta) and the strain front at velocity unity; the Abstract, printed p.299, states that the coupled equations 'are both hyperbolic' and that the infinite propagation velocity is eliminated
conditions_stated_by_source: not found. No sign or stability condition on tau0, k or the elastic constants is stated in the pages read (printed pp.299-304, 306-307 and 309); the paper only remarks that the relaxation constant beta becomes very small at high temperature (printed p.304) and that the general theory then reduces to the classical coupled theory.
dissipation_statement: not found. The paper nowhere says whether the theory is dissipative or not; printed p.303 mentions only that phonons and free electrons 'undergo collisions of a lossful nature, giving rise to thermal resistance', which is a physical mechanism, not a statement about the theory.

heat_law_in_words: (4.11)2: q_i = -theta0 (b_i dtheta/dt + k_ij theta_,j). The heat flux carries a temperature-rate term through b_i and a gradient term through k_ij, the latter being the Fourier part; (4.6) is the general form that also contains a_i, a_irs and the temperature-rate coefficient alpha b_i.
relaxation_parameters: not found. No relaxation time is named or symbolized anywhere in printed pp.1-7 and the word relaxation does not occur in the text; the rate term is carried by the coefficient b_i and by the combination h = f - b_i beta that appears in (4.10) and (4.14).
wave_speed_or_dispersion_ref: not found as an explicit formula: no wave speed and no dispersion relation is printed in pp.1-7. The Abstract (printed p.1) and Introduction (printed p.1) state only that the theory admits the possibility of second sound.

theory_name: Re-examination of the basic postulates of thermomechanics; heat flow in a stationary rigid solid of types I, II and III, types II and III being thermal-wave theories
heat_law_equation_ref: type I: eq (8.7c), printed p.184; type II: eqs (8.13), (8.17), (8.18), (8.19a,b) and (8.20), printed pp.185-186; type III: eqs (8.37) and (8.39), printed p.188; Cattaneo's equation, unnumbered display, printed p.187
heat_law_in_words: Type I reduces to Fourier's law q = -k grad theta, (8.7c), and to the heat equation rho c dtheta/dt = rho r + k laplacian theta, (8.8). Type II sets p b = -k rho beta, (8.18a), with beta = grad alpha the thermal displacement gradient, so the entropy flux is proportional to beta and not to the temperature gradient; with q = theta p by (7.25) and (8.6) the linear equation is c b d2T/dt2 = dr/dt + (k a / b) laplacian T, (8.20), which is a wave equation. Type III uses q = theta p = -(f1 beta + f2 gamma), (8.37), which gives the Jeffreys-type equation (8.39). Cattaneo's equation tau dq/dt + q = -k grad theta is printed on p.187.
relaxation_parameters: The only relaxation symbol is tau, and it occurs only inside Cattaneo's equation tau dq/dt + q = -k grad theta, unnumbered, printed p.187, which the paper calls 'Cattaneo's (1948) equation'. tau is not named a relaxation time and is not used in the authors' own type I-III constitutive equations; no relaxation time is attached to the type II or type III laws.
wave_speed_or_dispersion_ref: printed p.186: for type II with xi = 0 and k > 0, (8.20) is a standard wave equation and 'heat is propagated without damping with a wave speed (ak/cb^2)^(1/2)'; printed p.187: with d1 > 0 and b3 > 0, (8.28) is a telegraph equation whose solution transmits thermal waves 'with speed (k/b3)^(1/2) which are attenuated'
conditions_stated_by_source: 'the specific heat c must be non-negative, i.e. c >= 0' (printed p.184, from (9.14)); 'the conductivity coefficient must be non-negative, i.e. k >= 0' (printed p.185, from (8.11) and q = -k grad theta); (8.26) 'k d1 >= 0, b2 b - b3 d1 >= 0' (printed p.186); a > 0 and b > 0 in (8.17), printed p.185
dissipation_statement: printed p.186: type II heat is 'propagated without damping'; printed p.187: the telegraph equation transmits waves that 'are attenuated', while with b2 = 0 (8.28) 'gives a wave without damping', and if d1 = 0 then 'no restriction arises from thermodynamics on the sign of k'. The Second Law enters only as cyclic inequalities (9.11)-(9.12), printed p.190, and (9.14), printed p.191.

source_doi: 10.1007/BF00044969 (DOI not printed in this scan; carried over unchanged from the batch 001 record of the same paper)
theory_name: Thermoelasticity type I (classical, Fourier conduction) and type II (thermoelasticity without energy dissipation)
heat_law_equation_ref: type I: eq (2.38)3, printed p.197; type II: eq (3.9)3 and eq (3.13)3, printed pp.200-201
heat_law_in_words: Type I: p = -(kappa/theta0) grad theta, (2.38)3, with q = theta p, which after linearization is Fourier conduction with conductivity kappa. Type II: p = -dpsi/dPi, (3.9)3, and in the linearized isotropic case p = -(kappa*/theta0) Pi, (3.13)3, where Pi = grad alpha is the thermal displacement gradient; the flux then follows from the free-energy potential instead of the temperature gradient, and the heat flux is q = theta p.
relaxation_parameters: not found. No relaxation time and no relaxation function appears in the pages read (printed pp.189-203); the extra thermal constant is kappa* (printed as x* in the scan), introduced in (3.12), printed p.201, and described only as 'a constant'.
wave_speed_or_dispersion_ref: No wave-speed formula and no dispersion relation is printed in the pages read (printed pp.189-203). Printed p.202, after (3.17): under c > 0, kappa* >= 0 and lambda + 2 mu >= 0 the system (3.15)-(3.16) 'permit propagation of harmonic waves without damping'; the Abstract (printed p.189) and Introduction (printed p.190) state that heat is transmitted as thermal waves at finite speed.
conditions_stated_by_source: 'it can be shown that c >= 0 and kappa >= 0' (printed p.198, type I, from the Second Law); 'c > 0, kappa* >= 0, lambda + 2 mu >= 0', (3.17), printed p.202, type II; printed p.201 notes that c >= 0 follows from the Second Law and that 'no additional Second Law restrictions can be found since phi = 0 in the present development'
dissipation_statement: type II 'involves no dissipation of energy' (printed p.198); 'there is an absence of internal rate of production of entropy ... so that there is no dissipation of energy' (printed p.200); type I, by contrast, 'predicts propagation of waves with damping--the damping being due to the thermal part of the equations' (printed p.198)
